Description

Currently, when you link an Identity Provider to an Organization, it becomes unavailable for other Organizations or users that are not a member of any Organization. I believe Keycloak either shouldn't be disabling the provider elsewhere, or having the ability to flag the identity provider as shared in someway should be possible.

 Discussion

 

 Motivation

We offer Microsoft and Google social login. Currently some of our customer's organizations users have signed in with the the social provider, and others used built in account.

Some customers are now wanting to mandate Google or Microsoft based logins for their users onto our platform. If I tie our existing Microsoft/Google Identity Provider to their Organization, it becomes unavailable for other organizations and for non-organization users.

If I need to add duplicate Identity Providers for Google/Microsoft that are going to be specific to an Organization, then those users who already logged in via our existing social providers have to relink their accounts to the new Identity Provider. To them, they are already using either Google or Microsoft so is confusing and a little burdensome. 

 Details

I trust keycloak developer's and community's judgement on this, everything else has been solid. The only thing I could think of that may be the path of least resistance is to be able to indicate if an Identity Provider is 'shared'

- if an identity provider is specific to an organization, shared being false would mean it disappears as a provider option anywhere else. This is the current behavior.
- if an identity provider shared is true, then it can stay available for other Organizations or non-organization based login, and the 'hide on login page' can be used to control which option is shown for organization and non-organization based login.

This issue is about support for the delegation as mentioned in the token exchange specification. The most relevant specification sections:
- 
- 
- 
- (Example. It is in the end of the specs, but maybe best to start with to grasp what the delegation is about)

 Notes and considerations

Some random notes here for now. Comments welcome on this issue about the possible use-cases and if the notes from here makes sense to cover your particular use-case.

- Delegation is IMO better and safer than "subject impersonation" (subject impersonation is the case when the token sub is required to be changed) due to this:
 - The delegation does not change the sub claim. So the exchanged token still has same user in the sub claim as the original subject_token had.
 - The great thing is, that exchanged token from the delegation contains both sub and act claims. Hence the exchanged token has all the informations like This token has subject of user "normal-user", but the actor using this token is "admin-user" . It gives some additional info to resource-server applications as they can differentiate between the case when the token is:
 - Normal token issued to the sub user where the actor is really the sub user (Normal use-case)
 - Delegated token with both sub and act claims where the application knows that actor is really the admin user.

- Do we need to support delegation just with requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token ? Or do we need to support also refresh tokens? Access tokens are easier and more safe IMO and can be nice if we can start just with supporting those (unless there are requirements for refresh tokens)

- Do we want to allow the delegation just if the may_act claim is present in the subject_token as shown in the example in the token exchange specification (link above)? It will be nice if we can start with requiring may_act claim IMO

- Question is, how is the may_act claim created in the subject token in the first place? Note that this is even before the token-exchange request itself (as it is relevant to issuing the subject_token during initial authentication). I can see some potential for "dynamic client scopes" (which are experimental feature at the time of this writing).

- I guess that in many cases, it could be great to show the consent screen to the user like Grant admin user to act on your behalf during initial authentication. It can be perhaps useful if this consent screen is shown even if client has Consent Required OFF 
 
 Example delegation scenario 

1) Initial authentication is done by user user . The initial OIDC request will contain something like scope=may_act:admin (would require dynamic client scopes)

- The consent screen is shown to the user Grant user 'admin' to act on your behalf (optional)

- The client scope may_act would contain some protocol mapper, which will add the may_act claim to the subject-token for user admin

2) User admin authenticates in the meantime to receive his own token (later being used as actor_token)

3) The token-exchange request is sent with subject_token=subject-token-from-step-1&actor_token=admin-token-from-step-2

4) Token exchange request would need to verify both subject_token and actor_token . Besides normal verifications of actor_token (session exists, user exists and is enabled etc), it should be verified that actor_token subject MUST be the same as subject_token subject from may_act claim. Verified tokens added as notes to KeycloakSession (ideal is if we don't need to persist subject_token and actor_token into clientSession)

5) Some protocol mapper, which will add act claim to the exchanged token as long as verified subject_token and actor_token are present in the KeycloakSession. In case of exchanging to refresh-tokens, some claim should be added to the isseued refreshToken, so that further refreshes of that refresh-token can add act claim as well.
kept_issues.body:
This issue is about support for the delegation as mentioned in the token exchange specification. The most relevant specification sections:
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8693#name-delegation-vs-impersonation
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8693#name-act-actor-claim
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8693#name-may_act-authorized-actor-cl
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8693#name-delegation-token-exchange-e (Example. It is in the end of the specs, but maybe best to start with to grasp what the delegation is about)

## Notes and considerations

Some random notes here for now. Comments welcome on this issue about the possible use-cases and if the notes from here makes sense to cover your particular use-case.

- Delegation is IMO better and safer than "subject impersonation" (subject impersonation is the case when the token `sub` is required to be changed) due to this:
  - The delegation does not change the `sub` claim. So the exchanged token still has same user in the `sub` claim as the original `subject_token` had.
  - The great thing is, that exchanged token from the delegation contains both `sub` and `act` claims. Hence the exchanged token has all the informations like `This token has subject of user "normal-user", but the actor using this token is "admin-user"` . It gives some additional info to resource-server applications as they can differentiate between the case when the token is:
    - Normal token issued to the `sub` user where the actor is really the `sub` user (Normal use-case)
    - Delegated token with both `sub` and `act` claims where the application knows that actor is really the admin user.

- Do we need to support delegation just with `requested_token_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:token-type:access_token` ? Or do we need to support also refresh tokens? Access tokens are easier and more safe IMO and can be nice if we can start just with supporting those (unless there are requirements for refresh tokens)

- Do we want to allow the delegation just if the `may_act` claim is present in the `subject_token` as shown in the example in the token exchange specification (link above)? It will be nice if we can start with requiring `may_act` claim IMO

- Question is, how is the `may_act` claim created in the subject token in the first place? Note that this is even before the token-exchange request itself (as it is relevant to issuing the `subject_token` during initial authentication). I can see some potential for "dynamic client scopes" (which are experimental feature at the time of this writing).

- I guess that in many cases, it could be great to show the consent screen to the user like `Grant admin user to act on your behalf` during initial authentication. It can be perhaps useful if this consent screen is shown even if client has `Consent Required` OFF 
 
### Example delegation scenario 

1) Initial authentication is done by user `user` . The initial OIDC request will contain something like `scope=may_act:admin` (would require dynamic client scopes)

- The consent screen is shown to the user `Grant user 'admin' to act on your behalf` (optional)

- The client scope `may_act` would contain some protocol mapper, which will add the `may_act` claim to the subject-token for user `admin`

2) User `admin` authenticates in the meantime to receive his own token (later being used as `actor_token`)

3) The token-exchange request is sent with `subject_token=subject-token-from-step-1&actor_token=admin-token-from-step-2`

4) Token exchange request would need to verify both `subject_token` and `actor_token` . Besides normal verifications of `actor_token` (session exists, user exists and is enabled etc), it should be verified that `actor_token` subject MUST be the same as `subject_token` subject from `may_act` claim. Verified tokens added as notes to `KeycloakSession` (ideal is if we don't need to persist `subject_token` and `actor_token` into clientSession)

5) Some protocol mapper, which will add `act` claim to the exchanged token as long as verified `subject_token` and `actor_token` are present in the KeycloakSession. In case of exchanging to refresh-tokens, some claim should be added to the isseued refreshToken, so that further refreshes of that refresh-token can add `act` claim as well.
kept_issues.title: Support for token-exchange delegation

Description

When an administrator invites a member to an organization via the "Organizations" section in the Keycloak Admin Console, and the invited user does not yet exist in Keycloak, an invitation email is sent with an expiration time. However, there is currently no way to track these pending invitations within Keycloak once they are sent. Since the user hasn’t been created yet, there’s no record tied to an existing user, and administrators lose visibility into which invitations remain unaccepted or have expired.

I propose adding a feature to the "Organizations" section of the Admin Console to display a list of pending invitations for each organization, including:

- Email Address: The email address of the invited user.
- Invitation Sent Date: The date and time when the invitation was sent.
- Expiration Status: Whether the invitation link is still valid.
- Acceptance Status: Whether the invitation has been accepted (e.g., "Pending" or "Accepted").

 Discussion

_No response_

 Motivation

This would allow administrators to monitor outstanding invitations, resend them if needed, or clean up expired ones, improving the management of organization onboarding.

 Details

_No response_

### Description

This RFE is about adding more details when the admin-event is logged by the `JBossLoggingEventListenerProvider` . 

The possible suggestion is to:
- Doublecheck that in case that adminEvent contains some `details` (Field `AdminEvent.details`), those details are logged by the JBoss-logging listener to the server.log. It seems that it already works like that based on the commit https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/commit/0a05ba49 , but it will be good to doublecheck.

- Possibility to optionally log the representation for the admin events. In case that event has representation, it can be good to have some option to log the representation to the server.log. This will need to be explicitly enabled by the SPI switch during server startup. Maybe with something like this:
```
./kc.sh start --spi-events-listener-jboss-logging-enable-representation=true
```
It should be disabled by default as the field "representation" could be very big (especially for some cases like for example updating realm) . We should document that it should be used with care due to the big representation. Also there is a risk that some sensitive data might be leaked from the representation in the server.log, so we should maybe document this risk. In case that event-store is doing some sanitization of some representation fields, the jboss-logging implementation should make this sanitization as well.

Description

Admin REST API is a key part of Keycloak. Nearly every configuration interface (UI, CLI, Operator, …) uses it as its backend. As it evolved over the years of Keycloak’s existence, it needed to cover more and more areas with an increasing number of use cases and types of API clients. This explosive growth led to many design issues and inconsistencies making it difficult or sometimes even impossible for the API clients to use it for certain scenarios.

A new version of Admin API will aim to resolve the issues.

 Goals
 Blueprint for the new API
 Includes designs and prototypes for proofing them.
 Focused on the Keycloak Clients area as that will be the first to get implemented.
 Designs and prototypes cover all use cases of the API. That includes:

 Docs

 Implementation of the new API
 Created as v2
 Current Admin API (which will be marked as v1) will coexist with it it
 Will be done incrementally.
 Area by area, with each area also being implemented iteratively.
 Won’t clash with v1, v1 and v2 can be used side by side so users can gradually migrate as new areas are implemented.
 This applies both for the API itself and its clients too.
 Deprecation of the v1 API.

This is an umbrella issue for tracking the long-term effort for Admin API v2. The list of sub-issues will be updated over time.

The current API is suffering from many design issues. Fixing those issues requires redesigning the API from scratch as it is not viable to fix the existing API due to how extensive the changes need to be.

kept_issues.body:
### Description

Some platform needs `curl` to do healthchecks. They'll use the Docker image itself and run the healthcheck inside the image.

A simple example might be Docker Compose where you want the following to work:

```
services:
  keycloak:
    image: quay.io/keycloak/keycloak:26.1.3
    ports:
      - "8081:8080"
    environment:
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_USERNAME: "admin"
      KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD: "admin"
    command: start-dev
    volumes:
      - keycloak_data:/opt/keycloak/data/
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "curl", "-f", "http://localhost:8080/"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 5s
      start_period: 30s
      retries: 20
```

There is a [discussion over here](https://gist.github.com/sarath-soman/5d9aec06953bbd0990c648605d4dba07) looking at other ways of doing it, but all of those seem wildly impractical, and it seems like it would make more sense for this to just ship with the image.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Motivation

It should be easy to setup health checks, some platforms require `curl` (or a similar command) to exist in the Docker image to perform health checks (Docker Compose, Docker Swarm, etc).

### Details

Add `curl` as an package to the official Docker image.

Description

Currently, Keycloak does not provide a way to grant a user read-only administrative access to all existing realms and automatically extend this access to any realms created in the future. The only global roles available are admin and create-realm, and realm-specific roles must be assigned manually for each realm. This limitation makes it difficult to manage organization-wide audit, reporting, or monitoring users who require consistent, read-only access across all realms.

 Discussion

_No response_

 Motivation

- Centralized Audit and Monitoring: Organizations often need to grant security, audit, or monitoring teams read-only access to all realms for compliance, troubleshooting, or reporting.
- Operational Efficiency: Manually assigning roles for each new realm is error-prone and does not scale in environments with frequent realm creation and deletion.
- Consistency: Ensures that read-only users always have up-to-date access, reducing risk of missed realms and inconsistent permissions.

 Details

 Proposed Solution
- Introduce a new global admin role (e.g., global-read-only-admin) in the master realm.
- This role would grant read-only access (equivalent to view- roles) for all current and future realms, including the ability to view configuration, users, clients, and other realm resources without making modifications.
- The role should automatically apply to any realms created after assignment, without requiring manual updates.

Alternatives Considered
 • Current workaround is to manually assign view- roles for each realm client in the master realm and repeat this process for every new realm. This is not scalable and introduces operational overhead.

This feature would align with best practices for RBAC in large-scale, multi-tenant environments and is a common requirement in enterprise deployments.

### Description

Currently, Keycloak does not provide a way to grant a user read-only administrative access to all existing realms and automatically extend this access to any realms created in the future. The only global roles available are `admin` and `create-realm`, and realm-specific roles must be assigned manually for each realm. This limitation makes it difficult to manage organization-wide audit, reporting, or monitoring users who require consistent, read-only access across all realms.

### Discussion

_No response_

### Motivation

- **Centralized Audit and Monitoring**: Organizations often need to grant security, audit, or monitoring teams read-only access to all realms for compliance, troubleshooting, or reporting.
- **Operational Efficiency**: Manually assigning roles for each new realm is error-prone and does not scale in environments with frequent realm creation and deletion.
- **Consistency**: Ensures that read-only users always have up-to-date access, reducing risk of missed realms and inconsistent permissions.

### Details

 **Proposed Solution**
- Introduce a new global admin role (e.g., `global-read-only-admin`) in the master realm.
- This role would grant read-only access (equivalent to `view-*` roles) for all current and future realms, including the ability to view configuration, users, clients, and other realm resources without making modifications.
- The role should automatically apply to any realms created after assignment, without requiring manual updates.

**Alternatives Considered**
	•	Current workaround is to manually assign `view-*` roles for each realm client in the master realm and repeat this process for every new realm. This is not scalable and introduces operational overhead.

This feature would align with best practices for RBAC in large-scale, multi-tenant environments and is a common requirement in enterprise deployments.

Description

This feature proposes encrypting sensitive materials (e.g., private keys, secrets) managed by Keycloak’s ImportedKeyProvider and GeneratedKeyProvider classes before persisting them to the database. Currently, these materials are stored in plaintext, exposing them to risks if the database is compromised. The encryption would leverage a configurable secret key (e.g., from a VaultProvider, KeyStore, environment variable, or file) to ensure confidentiality at rest.

References:
- 

 Discussion

_No response_

 Motivation

The motivation for this feature stems from several key factors:

1. Security Best Practices: Sensitive cryptographic materials should never be stored in plaintext. Encryption mitigates risks of unauthorized access to keys, which could lead to impersonation, data breaches, or token forgery.

2. Compliance Requirements: Regulations like GDPR mandate encryption of sensitive data. Keycloak’s current lack of encryption for KeyProvider materials creates compliance hurdles.

3. Zero-Trust Posture: Encrypting keys aligns with zero-trust principles, ensuring that even if the database is breached, attackers cannot misuse stored secrets without the encryption key.

4. User Demand: Many organizations using Keycloak in regulated industries explicitly require encryption for secrets at rest.

5. I like that: 😎

 Details

The proposed feature is designed to be implemented in a backward-compatible manner, ensuring that existing key provider implementations continue to function without modification, while also providing a clear migration path for administrators to enable encryption for existing key materials. Flexibility to support different encryption algorithms in the future is also incorporated.

1. Encryption Design:

 - A symmetric encryption algorithm (e.g., AES-GCM) is used to encrypt private keys and secret materials before storing them in the database.
 - A new boolean configuration property encrypted is introduced in the COMPONENT_CONFIG table to indicate whether the key material is encrypted.
 - Key materials stored in the COMPONENT_CONFIG table currently exist in various formats. A standard format, such as JWE (JSON Web Encryption) or PKCS8, will be adopted for encrypted materials to ensure consistency and ease of decryption.
 - A new string configuration property encryptionKeyAlias is introduced in the COMPONENT_CONFIG table to store the alias of the encryption key.
 - The VaultProvider retrieves the encryption key, avoiding plaintext storage in the database. The alias stored in COMPONENT_CONFIG references the encryption key in the configured vault provider.

2. Affected Components:

 - KeyProvider Implementations: The following classes (and other relevant classes) will be modified to encrypt/decrypt secrets during persistence/retrieval:
 - GeneratedAesKeyProvider
 - GeneratedEcdhKeyProvider
 - GeneratedEcdsaKeyProvider
 - GeneratedEddsaKeyProvider
 - GeneratedHmacKeyProvider
 - ImportedRsaKeyProvider
 - Database Schema: No schema changes are required, but the COMPONENT_CONFIG table will store new properties for each key provider:
 - encrypted: boolean (default: false)
 - encryptionKeyAlias: string (used only if encrypted is true)

3. Migration Strategy:

 - Migration steps:
 1. The encrypted property is inferred as false for existing keys. If unset, the material is treated as unencrypted.
 2. When enabling encryption (setting encrypted to true), the administrator is required to provide the encryptionKeyAlias via a vault provider.
 3. Upon configuration, the key material is encrypted and stored in the database with the encryptionKeyAlias.

4. Changing Already Encrypted Keys:

 - To change the encryption key, the encryptionKeyAlias is updated to a new value. Existing materials are decrypted with the old key and re-encrypted with the new key. Both keys must be temporarily available in the vault provider.

5. Algorithm Flexibility:

 - Initial support for AES-GCM will be provided. The design accommodates future algorithms (e.g., ChaCha20). The chosen algorithm is stored in the key material (via JWE or PKCS8), enabling backward-compatible additions.

_No response_

With a huge user base it is not feasible to have admin users to manually remove OTPs on a separate communication channel (like telephone / mail).

 Details

I think the best option would be to use the other factor to reset the OTP meaning. A separate reset flow based on email flow that do not require the password to be reset.

Description

At present, Keycloak offers built-in support only for Google reCAPTCHA to protect public forms (such as login, registration, and forgotten password). While reCAPTCHA is widely used, it introduces multiple concerns:

 Privacy: reCAPTCHA collects user data and is not privacy-friendly by design.

 Vendor lock-in: relying solely on a single proprietary CAPTCHA provider contradicts the open-source philosophy of Keycloak.

 Compliance: in some regions (such as the EU), organizations may face compliance issues with Google services.

There are some community-contributed hCaptcha plugins, but they suffer from several problems:

 They are often outdated and no longer actively maintained.

 They require manual modifications to Keycloak themes or templates.

 They are fragile with Keycloak updates and frequently break compatibility, leading to maintenance overhead.

Proposal:

Please consider implementing native support for hCaptcha alongside reCAPTCHA in the official Keycloak distribution. This should ideally be configurable in the Admin Console in the same way as reCAPTCHA, without requiring any manual theme edits.

Why hCaptcha?

 hCaptcha is an open and privacy-friendly alternative to reCAPTCHA.

 It is widely adopted and provides a compatible challenge-response system.

 It allows organizations to comply with stricter privacy regulations.

 It aligns with Keycloak’s mission as an open-source identity provider by giving administrators freedom of choice.

Benefits:

 Reduces dependence on Google services.

 Improves compliance options for organizations in regulated sectors.

 Avoids the risks associated with outdated community plugins.

 Offers a straightforward way to enhance security without compromising privacy.

Suggested Implementation:

 Provide hCaptcha as a built-in feature selectable via the existing CAPTCHA configuration UI.

 Allow specifying the hCaptcha site key and secret key through the Admin Console.

 Ensure the server-side verification and client-side widget are fully integrated, just like reCAPTCHA.

 Make the feature optional and fully backward-compatible.

hcaptcha repo can be found here:

Currently, Keycloak supports events via Custom SPI (requires Java development).
Many modern identity providers (e.g., Auth0, Zitadel, Ory Hydra) offer webhooks to push events (e.g., user registration, login, profile updates) to external systems without writing code.

Add a built-in webhook system where admins can:

- Configure HTTP endpoints in the Keycloak Admin UI.
- Select events to forward (e.g., REGISTER, LOGIN, UPDATE_PROFILE).

- Sync user data to an external database without polling.
- Trigger workflows in serverless functions (e.g., AWS Lambda).
- Send real-time alerts on suspicious logins

Why This Matters

- Simpler integrations: No need to write/maintain custom listeners.
- Real-time updates: Better than polling.
- Competitive with SaaS: Matches Auth0, Okta, etc.

Description

(Thanks @mabartos for your input!)

 Summary proposal
- Enterprises that already rely on Keycloak for Identity & Access Management increasingly need governed lifecycle controls - approvals, segregation-of-duties, and auditability - without adopting an external IGA suite. 
- The community proof-of-concept at tide-foundation/keycloak-IGA shows that with a small set of changes we can embed basic IGA into the Keycloak core.
- This epic proposes upstreaming a minimal, optional IGA feature-set (hidden behind a feature flag) to satisfy those use-cases while keeping vanilla Keycloak lean.

---

 Walkthrough / demo 

 

 You can build and run the PoC yourself here: tide-foundation/keycloak-IGA
---
 Problem Statement 
Keycloak today applies changes to users, roles, and clients immediately. That is ideal for agility, but it leaves no native mechanism for:

 draft / approval workflows before high-impact changes go live, 
 role-assignment governance and composite-role life-cycle control, 
 quorum-based delegations that let multiple realm-admins approve critical updates, and 
 auditability of “who approved what, when” within Keycloak itself.

Organizations therefore bolt on external IGA platforms or write bespoke tooling, adding complexity and latency.

---

 Proposed Solution (high-level)

| Work-stream | Goal |
|-------------|------|
| 1. IGA MVP | Provide optional User, Realm, Client and Role providers that wrap existing JPA models with governance metadata and draft status. |
| 2. Drafting & Approval Workflow | Any change that modifies effective access is stored in a pending state until approved. |
| 3. Quorum & Delegation Engine | Realm-admins can be delegated; changes require a configurable percentage of current realm-admins (default 70 %). |
| 4. Admin UI & REST | Add a small console plugin and REST endpoints for viewing pending drafts, approving / rejecting, and viewing audit history. |
| 5. Migration & Compatibility | No schema changes unless the IGA profile is enabled; zero impact on existing deployments. |
| 6. Documentation & Operator Hooks | Describe how to enable the IGA profile in container images and the Keycloak Operator. |

---

 Non-Goals 

 Full-blown segregation-of-duties (SoD) policy modelling 
 Ticketing-system integrations 
 External provisioning (SCIM, HR feeds) 
 Reporting UI beyond basic audit-log export 

---

 Benefits 

 Security – Removes god-mode power from a single admin. 
 Compliance – Reduces audit findings where four-eyes approval of entitlements is mandatory. 
 Developer Experience – Keeps governance in the same platform and API developers already use. 
 Incremental Adoption – IGA profile can be enabled per realm or cluster for a phased rollout.

kept_issues.body:
### Description

(Thanks [@mabartos](https://github.com/mabartos) for your input!)

## Summary proposal
- Enterprises that already rely on Keycloak for Identity & Access Management increasingly need governed lifecycle controls - approvals, segregation-of-duties, and auditability - without adopting an external IGA suite.  
- The community proof-of-concept at **[tide-foundation/keycloak-IGA](https://github.com/tide-foundation/keycloak-IGA)** shows that with a small set of changes we can embed basic IGA into the Keycloak core.
- This epic proposes upstreaming a minimal, optional IGA feature-set (hidden behind a feature flag) to satisfy those use-cases while keeping vanilla Keycloak lean.

---

## Walkthrough / demo  

[![Native Keycloak IGA Walkthrough](http://img.youtube.com/vi/BrTBgFM7Lq0/0.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BrTBgFM7Lq0 "Native Keycloak IGA Walkthrough")

* [You can build and run the PoC yourself here: tide-foundation/keycloak-IGA](https://github.com/tide-foundation/keycloak-IGA)
---
## Problem Statement  
Keycloak today applies changes to users, roles, and clients immediately. That is ideal for agility, but it leaves no native mechanism for:

* draft / approval workflows before high-impact changes go live,  
* role-assignment governance and composite-role life-cycle control,  
* quorum-based delegations that let multiple realm-admins approve critical updates, and  
* auditability of “who approved what, when” within Keycloak itself.

Organizations therefore bolt on external IGA platforms or write bespoke tooling, adding complexity and latency.

---

## Proposed Solution (high-level)

| Work-stream | Goal |
|-------------|------|
| **1. IGA MVP** | Provide optional User, Realm, Client and Role providers that wrap existing JPA models with governance metadata and draft status. |
| **2. Drafting & Approval Workflow** | Any change that modifies effective access is stored in a pending state until approved. |
| **3. Quorum & Delegation Engine** | Realm-admins can be delegated; changes require a configurable percentage of current realm-admins (default 70 %). |
| **4. Admin UI & REST** | Add a small console plugin and REST endpoints for viewing pending drafts, approving / rejecting, and viewing audit history. |
| **5. Migration & Compatibility** | No schema changes unless the IGA profile is enabled; zero impact on existing deployments. |
| **6. Documentation & Operator Hooks** | Describe how to enable the IGA profile in container images and the Keycloak Operator. |

---

## Non-Goals  

* Full-blown segregation-of-duties (SoD) policy modelling  
* Ticketing-system integrations  
* External provisioning (SCIM, HR feeds)  
* Reporting UI beyond basic audit-log export  

---

## Benefits  

* **Security** – Removes god-mode power from a single admin.  
* **Compliance** – Reduces audit findings where four-eyes approval of entitlements is mandatory.  
* **Developer Experience** – Keeps governance in the same platform and API developers already use.  
* **Incremental Adoption** – IGA profile can be enabled per realm or cluster for a phased rollout.  
* **Community Alignment** – Builds on an existing OSS PoC, preventing ecosystem fragmentation.  

---

## References  

* [tide-foundation/keycloak-IGA](https://github.com/tide-foundation/keycloak-IGA) README (feature summary and SPI list)  
* Keycloak SPI developer guide  
* CNCF Security & Audit WG recommendations for least privilege and change control

### Discussion

https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/discussions/41350

_No response_

### Motivation

### Description

As of today AuthenticationManager provides a public method to log out all clients belonging to all user sessions of a given user:
```
AuthenticationManager::backchannelLogoutUserFromClient
```

In some authentication flow integrations it could come handy to only log out the client sessions belonging to a specific user session.

The method to be created could be used by the current implementation by iterating over all user sessions, and calling the to-be-implemented method.

Possibly it would be wise considering renaming the current method (as part of another issue), since the current name does not really describe that it takes all user sessions with all client sessions.

My suggestion is to add a new 
```
public static void backchannelLogoutUserFromClients(KeycloakSession session, RealmModel realm, UserSessionModel userSession, ClientModel client, UriInfo uriInfo, HttpHeaders headers)
```
method.

Than this new method could be proxied from the current one:
```
    // possibly backchannelLogoutUserFromAllClients would be more descriptive
    public static void backchannelLogoutUserFromClient(KeycloakSession session, RealmModel realm, UserModel user, ClientModel client, UriInfo uriInfo, HttpHeaders headers) {
        session.sessions().getUserSessionsStream(realm, user)
                .forEach(userSession -> backchannelLogoutUserFromClients(session, realm, userSession, ClientModel client, uriInfo, headers))
}
```

Description
Currently, the client setting “Always Display in UI” makes the client visible in the account console for all users, regardless of their roles or permissions. There is no option to restrict this behavior to only authorized users or roles.

 Discussion
This design limits flexibility. Administrators may want certain clients (e.g., security-admin-console) to be permanently visible for specific users or roles, while preventing unnecessary clutter or exposure for others. At present, the only workarounds are creating duplicate clients or customizing the account console theme, both of which increase complexity and maintenance burden.

 Motivation
Provide a more fine-grained control over client visibility in the account console. This will improve both usability and security:

Usability: authorized users can always find critical applications, even when not in an active session.

Security: non-authorized users will not see sensitive clients displayed unnecessarily.

 Details
Add an additional option next to “Always Display in UI”, such as:

“Always display in UI for authorized users/roles only”

When enabled, the client will be shown in the account console only for users who have roles or permissions mapped to that client. Other users will not see the client unless they meet the authorization conditions. This option would extend existing functionality without breaking backward compatibility.

Description

Keycloak currently supports using JWTs for client authentication (client assertions). However, the client assertion has to be self-signed by the client and can not be issued by a 3rd party.

Supporting client assertions issued by a 3rd party would support federated client authentication. This opens up the door for the following use-cases:

 Enabling clients to authenticate with Keycloak using a Kubernetes Service Account
 Enabling clients to authenticate with SPIFFE JWT SVIDs
 Enabling clients to authenticate with Keycloak using credentials associated with a different IdP

A realm admin would first configure a trust relationship (identity provider) between a realm and an 3rd party that can issue client assertion tokens. Once configured clients can be configured to use federated JWT authentication and select the trust relationship (identity provider) and provide the external client id (subject claim value).

 Value Proposition

Federated client authentication opens up the door for authenticating clients without credentials, or reducing the amount of credentials a client needs to handle.

 Goals

 Support client assertions issued by 3rd party providers for OpenID Connect clients
 Support SPIFFE JWT SVIDs
 Support Kubernetes Service Accounts

 Non-Goals

 Support X.509 authentication (SPIFFE X.509 SVIDs, SAML clients, etc.); at some point in the future we may introduce a concept of a certificate authority trust relationship to improve configuration of mTLS authentication for clients
 Support auto-registration or dynamic registration of clients; this will be a follow-up at a later point

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

Instead of adding a different concept of 3rd party trust in a realm this should be based on identity providers. This allows a single trust relationship to provide one or more aspects, as well as central management of trust relationships within a realm.

Requirements for client assertions:

 Must be a JWS signed with the keys from the identity provider
 iss must match identity provider issuer URL; required unless sub is a URI including the issuer
 sub claim must match the external subject configured for the client; if a URI (for example spiffe://trust-domain/workload-id) and no iss claim is present the scheme and authority is used as the iss value
 aud claim must be a single value equal to the realm issuer URL
 exp claim required; must be in the future
 nbf claim optional; if present must be in the past
 iat claim optional; if present must be a maximum of 300 seconds in the past
 jti required and must be unique if re-use is not permitted by identity provider; if re-use is permitted jti is optional
kept_issues.body:
### Description

Keycloak currently supports using JWTs for client authentication (client assertions). However, the client assertion has to be self-signed by the client and can not be issued by a 3rd party.

Supporting client assertions issued by a 3rd party would support federated client authentication. This opens up the door for the following use-cases:

* Enabling clients to authenticate with Keycloak using a Kubernetes Service Account
* Enabling clients to authenticate with SPIFFE JWT SVIDs
* Enabling clients to authenticate with Keycloak using credentials associated with a different IdP

A realm admin would first configure a trust relationship (identity provider) between a realm and an 3rd party that can issue client assertion tokens. Once configured clients can be configured to use federated JWT authentication and select the trust relationship (identity provider) and provide the external client id (subject claim value).

### Value Proposition

Federated client authentication opens up the door for authenticating clients without credentials, or reducing the amount of credentials a client needs to handle.

### Goals

* Support [client assertions](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7521) issued by 3rd party providers for OpenID Connect clients
* Support [SPIFFE JWT SVIDs](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-schwenkschuster-oauth-spiffe-client-auth/)
* Support Kubernetes Service Accounts

### Non-Goals

* Support X.509 authentication (SPIFFE X.509 SVIDs, SAML clients, etc.); at some point in the future we may introduce a concept of a certificate authority trust relationship to improve configuration of mTLS authentication for clients
* Support auto-registration or dynamic registration of clients; this will be a follow-up at a later point

### Discussion

_No response_

### Notes

Instead of adding a different concept of 3rd party trust in a realm this should be based on identity providers. This allows a single trust relationship to provide one or more aspects, as well as central management of trust relationships within a realm.

Requirements for client assertions:

* Must be a JWS signed with the keys from the identity provider
* `iss` must match identity provider issuer URL; required unless `sub` is a URI including the issuer
* `sub` claim must match the external subject configured for the client; if a URI (for example `spiffe://trust-domain/workload-id`) and no `iss` claim is present the scheme and authority is used as the `iss` value
* `aud` claim must be a single value equal to the realm issuer URL
* `exp` claim required; must be in the future
* `nbf` claim optional; if present must be in the past
* `iat` claim optional; if present must be a maximum of 300 seconds in the past
* `jti` required and must be unique if re-use is not permitted by identity provider; if re-use is permitted `jti` is optional
kept_issues.title: Federated client authentication

Description

Currently, when a user is presented with a consent screen that includes optional client scopes, they have two choices: grant consent to all scopes (required and optional) or deny consent entirely. There is no way for a user to selectively approve some optional scopes while rejecting others.

This "all or nothing" approach forces users to either accept scopes they might not be comfortable with or lose access to the client application altogether.

Proposed Feature
I propose adding a mechanism to the consent screen that allows users to individually select or deselect each optional client scope before granting consent. Required scopes would remain mandatory and could be displayed as checked and disabled.

This could look something like this:

Application 'My Cool App' is requesting the following permissions:

✅ email (required)

✅ profile (required)

☑️ Read your photos (optional) - User can uncheck this

☑️ Manage your calendar (optional) - User can uncheck this

 Discussion

_No response_

 Motivation

Why is this important?
Enhanced User Control & Privacy 🔐: This feature would give users granular control over their data, allowing them to make informed decisions about what information they share with an application.

Principle of Least Privilege: It encourages applications to follow the principle of least privilege by allowing users to grant only the permissions that are absolutely necessary for the functionality they intend to use.

Improved User Trust: Giving users this level of control can significantly increase their trust in both the application and the Keycloak-powered identity system.

Regulatory Compliance: It aligns better with the data minimization principles of privacy regulations like GDPR, which emphasize collecting only the data that is strictly necessary.

This feature would be a significant step forward in making Keycloak an even more user-centric and privacy-focused identity and access management solution.

Description

Currently, the Organizations feature provides excellent multi-tenancy support for managing users, identity providers. However, this multi-tenancy does not extend to OAuth2/OIDC clients. Clients can only be created and managed at the realm level by a realm administrator.

This limitation creates a significant bottleneck in SaaS environments. As a SaaS provider, we want to empower our tenants (Organizations) to self-manage the applications they integrate with our service. For example, a tenant might want to:

Integrate their own internal scripts or services with our APIs using the OAuth2 Client Credentials flow.

Configure a specific OIDC client for their own internal web application.

Manage client secrets and redirect URIs without needing to file a support ticket with us (the realm administrators).

Without this capability, all client management becomes a manual, centralized task that hinders tenant autonomy and scalability.

 Value Proposition

I propose enhancing the Organizations feature to allow organizations to create, configure, and manage their own OAuth2/OIDC clients.

This could be implemented as follows:

A "Clients" Tab in the Organization UI: A new "Clients" section would be added to the organization's administration console, similar to the one at the realm level.

Delegated Permissions: A new set of permissions (e.g., manage-org-clients, view-org-clients) would be created that can be assigned to organization administrators. This would give them the authority to manage clients only within their own organization.

Client Isolation: Clients created by an organization would be scoped to and owned by that organization. A realm administrator would have visibility over all clients, but an organization administrator would only see the clients belonging to their organization.

Policy and Template Control (Optional but ideal): Realm administrators could define policies or client templates that constrain the types of clients an organization can create (e.g., allowed grant types, default scopes, protocol settings).

Example User Story:

As an Administrator of "Company A" (an Organization in Keycloak), I want to register and manage my own OIDC clients so that I can securely connect our internal applications to the main service without relying on the service provider's administrators.

 Goals

The primary goal is to delegate client management to Organization Administrators, enabling true self-service for tenants within a multi-tenant Keycloak deployment. This enhances scalability, autonomy, and security.

Core Capabilities for an Organization Administrator
An Organization Administrator, with the appropriate permissions, should be able to perform the following actions exclusively on clients belonging to their own organization:

1. Full Client CRUD Operations:

Create: Register new OIDC/OAuth2 clients for their organization's applications (web apps, mobile apps, backend services).

Read: View a list of their organization's clients and inspect their configurations.

Update: Modify all standard client settings, such as names, descriptions, and protocol settings.

Delete: Remove clients that are no longer needed.

2. Client Authentication and Authorization Configuration:

Manage Client Secrets: View and regenerate secrets for clients using the client_secret_post or client_secret_basic authentication methods.

Configure Authentication: Set up other authentication methods like JWT with a private key.

Control Grant Types: Enable or disable flows like Authorization Code, Implicit, Client Credentials, etc., for their clients.

Set Redirect URIs: Manage the list of allowed redirect_uri patterns for their applications to ensure secure authentication flows.

3. Scope and Role Management:

Assign Scopes: Attach realm roles and client roles (from other clients) to their client's scope.

Manage Service Accounts: If a client has a service account, manage the roles assigned to that service account.

4. User Interface Integration:

Dedicated "Clients" Tab: Access all these capabilities through a new "Clients" section within their organization's view in the Keycloak Admin Console. The UI should be isolated, showing only their organization's clients.

 Non-Goals

To maintain realm security, stability, and clear separation of duties, this feature should not provide the following capabilities to Organization Administrators. These responsibilities must remain with the Realm Administrators.

1. No Management of Realm-Level Resources:

Realm Roles: Organization Administrators should not be able to create, edit, or delete realm-level roles. They can only assign existing, approved realm roles to their client scopes.

Authentication Flows: They cannot create, copy, or modify any authentication, registration, or reset-credential flows for the realm. These flows define the fundamental security posture of the entire realm.

Realm-Level Identity Providers: They cannot create or configure new Identity Providers for the entire realm. They can only use the IdPs that a Realm Administrator has explicitly enabled for their organization.

2. No Creation of Shared, Cross-Organization Resources:

Client Scopes: Organization Administrators should not be able to create new "Shared Client Scopes" that would be visible or usable by other organizations. They can only configure the scope for their own clients using predefined roles and mappers.

Protocol Mappers: They cannot create new protocol mappers or modify built-in ones. The ability to add custom mappers (especially script mappers) is a high-privilege operation and must remain with the Realm Administrator.

3. No Control Over Realm-Wide Policies and Security:

Client Policies: Organization Administrators are subject to Client Policies but cannot create, view, or modify them. This ensures the Realm Administrator can enforce security standards (e.g., token settings, required grant types) across all organizations.

Realm Keys: They will have no access to the realm's token signing keys or other cryptographic settings.

Token Lifespan: They cannot override the realm's default token lifespan settings. This must be controlled centrally by the Realm Administrator.

4. No "Escape" from Organizational Boundaries:

An administrator for "Organization A" must never be able to view, modify, or manage clients belonging to "Organization B" or clients that have no organization assigned. All actions must be strictly confined within their own organizational container.

_No response_

 Notes

_No response_

### Description

Currently, the Organizations feature provides excellent multi-tenancy support for managing users, identity providers. However, this multi-tenancy does not extend to OAuth2/OIDC clients. Clients can only be created and managed at the realm level by a realm administrator.

This limitation creates a significant bottleneck in SaaS environments. As a SaaS provider, we want to empower our tenants (Organizations) to self-manage the applications they integrate with our service. For example, a tenant might want to:



Integrate their own internal scripts or services with our APIs using the OAuth2 Client Credentials flow.

Configure a specific OIDC client for their own internal web application.

Manage client secrets and redirect URIs without needing to file a support ticket with us (the realm administrators).

Without this capability, all client management becomes a manual, centralized task that hinders tenant autonomy and scalability.

### Value Proposition

I propose enhancing the Organizations feature to allow organizations to create, configure, and manage their own OAuth2/OIDC clients.

This could be implemented as follows:

A "Clients" Tab in the Organization UI: A new "Clients" section would be added to the organization's administration console, similar to the one at the realm level.

Delegated Permissions: A new set of permissions (e.g., manage-org-clients, view-org-clients) would be created that can be assigned to organization administrators. This would give them the authority to manage clients only within their own organization.

Client Isolation: Clients created by an organization would be scoped to and owned by that organization. A realm administrator would have visibility over all clients, but an organization administrator would only see the clients belonging to their organization.

Example User Story:

Assign Scopes: Attach realm roles and client roles (from other clients) to their client's scope.

4. User Interface Integration:

Dedicated "Clients" Tab: Access all these capabilities through a new "Clients" section within their organization's view in the Keycloak Admin Console. The UI should be isolated, showing only their organization's clients.

### Non-Goals

To maintain realm security, stability, and clear separation of duties, this feature should not provide the following capabilities to Organization Administrators. These responsibilities must remain with the Realm Administrators.

1. No Management of Realm-Level Resources:

Realm Roles: Organization Administrators should not be able to create, edit, or delete realm-level roles. They can only assign existing, approved realm roles to their client scopes.

Description

The Spotless plugin could help maintain a consistent code style, reduce formatting-related review comments, and improve developer workflow. Once integrated, contributors would be able to format their code automatically before committing changes. .

 Value Proposition

- Automated code formatting ensures consistency and readability across the codebase.
- Reduces manual formatting efforts and streamlines code reviews.
- Helps new contributors easily align with project formatting standards.

 Goals

- Integrate Spotless plugin into the build process.
- Enforce formatting rules on Java and other supported languages.
- Require code to be formatted before merge (preferably via CI checks).
- Document how contributors should run the formatter locally.

 Non-Goals

- Changing existing code style rules, unless required by Spotless defaults.
- Enforcing formatting for languages not supported by Spotless.
- Replacing other quality tools unrelated to formatting.

 Notes

Implementation could include adding Spotless configuration to the Maven/Gradle build files and updating contribution guidelines to require formatting. See Spotless documentation for details.

The new authentication method

n/a

### Description

OAuth Identity and Authorization Chaining Across Domains enables applications to access resources across multiple trust domains.

This is done by utilising the following specifications:

* [OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc8693)
* [Assertion Framework for OAuth 2.0 Client Authentication and Authorization Grants](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7521)

A simplified view of the flow involved:
```mermaid
---
config:
    mirrorActors: false
---
sequenceDiagram
    box Domain A
    participant IDPA as External IdP
    participant C as Client
    end
    box Domain B
    participant IDPB as Keycloak
    participant RS as REST API
    end

    C->>IDPA: Exchange token
    IDPA->>C: Assertion
    C->>IDPB: Token request, with assertion
    IDPB->>C: Token response
    C->>RS: Request with token
```

### Value Proposition

This provides a better flow compared to Keycloak's token exchange for a few reasons:

* Clean separation - token exchange is used for internal tokens; while authorization grants are used for external tokens
* Standards based - even though the specification is a draft it builds on leveraging two final specifications, but the specification is seeing a lot of traction; including extensions built on-top of it like Identity Assertion Authorization Grant
* There is a clear trust relationship with both IdPs taking part of the cross-domain requests

End of the day Keycloak's token exchange for external to internal flows would require two requests; the client would first need to do a token exchange request to the local IdP to obtain a token with the external IdPs as the audience, and afterwards a second token exchange request to the external IdP to obtain a token with the external issuer and external audiences.

### Description

[Authorization Grants](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7521) opens up a lot of use-cases allowing applications that have tokens issued by a third-party to obtain access tokens issued by Keycloak.

Example use-cases include:

* Applications that authenticate with an external IdP can access resources secured by Keycloak
* Applications secured by Keycloak can access resources secured by an external IdP
* SaaS solutions can also provide access to resources through federation with an external IdP

A simplified view of the flow involved:

```mermaid
---
config:
    mirrorActors: false
---
sequenceDiagram
    box Domain A
    participant C as Client
    participant TS as Token Service
    participant KC as Keycloak
    participant RS as REST API
    end

    C->>TS: Request assertion
    TS->>C: Assertion
    C->>KC: Token request, with assertion
```

Description

Keycloak provides support for numerous database vendors, however we do not detail in our guides how any of these vendors should be deployed in Kubernetes and we leave this as a challenge for users to overcome.

Provisioning production-ready databases in Kubernetes is a complex undertaking due to the mismatch between stateless ephemeral containers and the stateful, persistent requirements of databases. Fortunately, there now exists many Apache 2.0 licensed projects which leverage Kubernetes Operators in order to manage these challenges for users. For example:

 CloudNativePG - Postgres
 Crunchy - Postgres
 Percona - MySQL, Postgres

In order to simplify deployment of Keycloak on Kubernetes environments, we should pick a preferred project and officially support this.

 Value Proposition

 Improve user experience by removing a barrier for Keycloak deployment on Kubernetes
 Reduce GitHub issues related to misconfiguration of databases on Kubernetes
 Increased portfolio integration (both Crunchy and Percona are available via Red Hat certified operators)

 Goals

 Support Kubernetes native version of an already supported database vendor, e.g. Postgres
 Determine which Kubernetes native database to support
 Document in Keycloak guides how to deploy Keycloak on Kubernetes with the database by using a scripted setup in the Keycloak main repo based on Minikube
 Benchmark Keycloak with database to determine minimal hardware requirements
 Write blog(s) to promote to the community

 Non-Goals

 Support additional database vendors in Keycloak
 Support horizontally scalable database, e.g. TiDB
 Have the full main CI test pipeline running against an Operator based database, as we assume it would "just" deploy a regular PostgreSQL that is similar enough. 
 Keycloak Operator deploys the database via CRs (might be future work)
 Describe backup and restore

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

Description

This issue is about introducing support for organization-specific groups. This capability will allow for the creation and management of groups that are scoped to a particular organization, rather than being global to the entire realm.

This feature is a foundational piece and the first step towards enabling self-service and delegated administration for organizations. It will provide the necessary structure for organization administrators to manage their users effectively.

 Value Proposition

In many B2B and multi-tenant scenarios, administrators of a specific organization need to manage their own users without affecting the global realm configuration. The introduction of organization-specific groups serves several immediate and critical use cases, even without the immediate inclusion of role management:

- Logical User Categorization and Management: It allows an organization's administrator to categorize their users into logical groups (e.g., engineering, sales, finance) that are meaningful only within the context of their own organization. This is a fundamental requirement for delegated user management.

To be decided if in-scope or not:

- Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) via Token Claims: Organization-specific groups can hold attributes. These attributes can be mapped to a user's token when they log in. Applications can then inspect these claims to make authorization decisions, effectively enabling an ABAC model where the application enforces the rules based on the attributes provided in the token. For example, a group auditors could have an attribute that, when present in a token, grants access to an audit log viewer in an external application.
 - What exists today: Keycloak has a powerful token mapping system. A realm administrator can configure a client's "Mappers" to add claims to a token. One of the standard mappers is the "Group Membership" mapper, and you can also map user or group attributes.
 - Q: Should we allow realm admin to use existing token mappers to pull information from newly available organization-specific groups in scope of this addition?

- Conditional Authentication and Policy Enforcement: Group membership is a powerful condition for authentication flows. With organization-specific groups, a realm administrator can define policies such as requiring members of a specific organization's finance group to use Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), while other users are not subject to the same requirement.
 - What exists today: Keycloak's authentication flows are highly customizable. A realm administrator can add "Conditional Authenticators" to any flow. One of the most common conditions is "Conditional User Group Membership".
 - Q: Should we allow realm admin to use existing conditional authenticators to change the login experience based on membership in the newly available organization-specific groups in scope of this addition?

 Goals

This feature will focus on providing the core group management capabilities within the scope of an organization.

What is included in this issue:

- API and UI support for creating, viewing, updating, and deleting groups scoped to an organization.

- The ability to add users to and remove users from these organization-specific groups.

- TBD

 Non-Goals

- Organization-specific Roles: The ability to attach org-specific roles to these groups is explicitly out of scope for this initial implementation. That functionality will be addressed in a subsequent issue. 

- Fine-Grained Admin Permissions (FGAP): Using these groups to delegate administrative permissions within Keycloak (e.g., allowing an organization admin to manage their own groups) is not part of this issue. This is a foundational step, and delegated administration will be built upon it in the future.

- Sub-Organizations: This implementation will support groups within an organization. The ability to create nested organizations is out of scope.

 Discussion

 

 Notes

### Description

This issue is about introducing support for organization-specific groups. This capability will allow for the creation and management of groups that are scoped to a particular organization, rather than being global to the entire realm.

This feature is a foundational piece and the first step towards enabling self-service and delegated administration for organizations. It will provide the necessary structure for organization administrators to manage their users effectively.

### Value Proposition

In many B2B and multi-tenant scenarios, administrators of a specific organization need to manage their own users without affecting the global realm configuration. The introduction of organization-specific groups serves several immediate and critical use cases, even without the immediate inclusion of role management:

- **Logical User Categorization and Management**: It allows an organization's administrator to categorize their users into logical groups (e.g., `engineering`, `sales`, `finance`) that are meaningful only within the context of their own organization. This is a fundamental requirement for delegated user management.

To be decided if in-scope or not:

- **Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) via Token Claims**: Organization-specific groups can hold attributes. These attributes can be mapped to a user's token when they log in. Applications can then inspect these claims to make authorization decisions, effectively enabling an ABAC model where the application enforces the rules based on the attributes provided in the token. For example, a group auditors could have an attribute that, when present in a token, grants access to an audit log viewer in an external application.
  - What exists today: Keycloak has a powerful token mapping system. A realm administrator can configure a client's "Mappers" to add claims to a token. One of the standard mappers is the "Group Membership" mapper, and you can also map user or group attributes.
  - Q: Should we allow realm admin to use existing token mappers to pull information from newly available organization-specific groups in scope of this addition?

- **Conditional Authentication and Policy Enforcement**: Group membership is a powerful condition for authentication flows. With organization-specific groups, a realm administrator can define policies such as requiring members of a specific organization's finance group to use Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA), while other users are not subject to the same requirement.
  - What exists today: Keycloak's authentication flows are highly customizable. A realm administrator can add "Conditional Authenticators" to any flow. One of the most common conditions is "Conditional User Group Membership".
  - Q: Should we allow realm admin to use existing conditional authenticators to change the login experience based on membership in the newly available organization-specific groups in scope of this addition?

### Goals

This feature will focus on providing the core group management capabilities within the scope of an organization.

What is included in this issue:

- API and UI support for creating, viewing, updating, and deleting groups scoped to an organization.

- The ability to add users to and remove users from these organization-specific groups.

- TBD

### Non-Goals

- **Organization-specific Roles**: The ability to attach org-specific roles to these groups is explicitly out of scope for this initial implementation. That functionality will be addressed in a subsequent issue. 

- **Fine-Grained Admin Permissions (FGAP)**: Using these groups to delegate administrative permissions within Keycloak (e.g., allowing an organization admin to manage their own groups) is not part of this issue. This is a foundational step, and delegated administration will be built upon it in the future.

- **Sub-Organizations**: This implementation will support groups within an organization. The ability to create nested organizations is out of scope.

### Discussion

https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/30180

### Notes

Description

The target of this milestone is the ability to handle assertions issued by particular social providers to be used as assertions in the RFC-7523 grant-type and issue Keycloak tokens based on that.

This milestone is follow-up to 43565 .

The social providers usually have limited capabilities than proper OAuth/OIDC providers and may not be able to issue proper JWT assertions. Some social providers does not event support JWT tokens at all. The ideal is, if assertion is JWT compliant with RFC-7523, but we might need to support also non-JWT tokens for particular social providers.

 Goals

- Support for social providers capable of mobile API login (Google social provider only. Apple is capable of doing mobile API login, but it is not supported in Keycloak as of now)

 Non-Goals

- Supporting other social providers (especially those, which are not capable of creating proper JWT assertion grant)

 Notes

_No response_

Description

Please provide an officially supported C/.NET SDK for Keycloak that covers the Admin REST API (realms, users, groups, roles, clients, identity providers, policies, attack-detection, etc.) and selected Management endpoints.
The SDK should expose typed models, async methods, and first-class .NET integration (DI, IHttpClientFactory, logging, configuration, and resilience).
Developers today must either hand-roll clients from raw HTTP/OpenAPI or rely on community libraries with uneven coverage and version lag. An official SDK would standardize integrations and reduce support issues caused by inconsistent implementations.

 Value Proposition

- Developer productivity: strongly typed models instead of untyped Map payloads; discoverable API surface with IntelliSense.
- Reliability: versioned releases aligned with Keycloak versions; tested compatibility, retries, and timeouts by default.
- Security & best practices: built-in auth flows (client credentials, PAT, token exchange) and guidance for secure configuration.
- Ecosystem alignment: first-party package simplifies adoption in .NET shops (ASP.NET Core, Azure, Kubernetes).
- Supportability: fewer GitHub issues caused by incorrect ad-hoc requests; easier docs and samples.

 Goals

- Ship a NuGet package (e.g., Keycloak.Admin.Sdk) targeting .NET 8/9.
- Cover core Admin API areas: realms, users, groups, roles, clients, client-scopes, auth-flows, sessions, user-storage, events, attack-detection.
- Provide typed DTOs for all responses (no opaque maps), using System.Text.Json (source-generated) for perf.
- Support pluggable auth: client credentials (service account), PAT, on-behalf-of/token exchange where applicable.
- Integrate with IServiceCollection and IHttpClientFactory (DI-friendly configuration, retries/timeout, logging).
- Provide resilience (Polly), paging helpers, and cancellation tokens everywhere.
- First-class .NET Aspire support:
 - Ready-to-use Aspire component/extension (e.g., builder.AddKeycloak("keycloak")) that wires:
 - typed options from Aspire’s appsettings/environment,
 - HttpClientFactory with resilience & OTel,
 - health checks/liveness/readiness for Keycloak connectivity,
 - service discovery & endpoint binding,
 - connection string/secret injection via Aspire secrets.
 - Samples for AppHost + service wiring, plus dashboards with OpenTelemetry traces/metrics.
 - Generate clients from the official OpenAPI with a small curated shim for underspecified parts; CI re-generates on each Keycloak release.
 - Include samples: user lifecycle, role mapping, brute-force status, import/export, IdP linking, realm management.

 Non-Goals

- Not a replacement for Java Admin Client.
- Not an OIDC middleware for app login (ASP.NET has native OIDC).
- No GUI/CLI in v1 (could come later).
- No support for end-of-life Keycloak versions.

 Discussion

There are community options (e.g., Kiota-generated clients, Keycloak.AuthServices, Keycloak.Net) but they vary in coverage and lag behind. An official SDK would provide canonical models, breaking-change guidance, and test matrices aligned to server versions.

 Notes

_No response_

Description

Support for the OpenID Shared Signals Framework enables the propagation of security relevant events among parties in a federated identity system.

 Value Proposition

Adding initial support for the OpenID Shared Signals Framework (SSF) enables Keycloak to participate in modern, interoperable security event sharing across federated identity systems.
This enhances Keycloak's ability to react to security incidents in near real-time, improving the overall security posture and trust between cooperating identity providers and relying parties.

 Goals

- Keycloak can act as a SSF Receiver
- Keycloak supports multiple SSF Receivers per realm
- keycloak can use streams of a SSF Transmitter
- Keycloak can validate and process RFC8417 Security Event Tokens (SETs)
- Initially Keycloak can support and process the following events (SSF Stream Updated, SSF Stream Verification, CAEP Session Revoked)
- Keycloak can map support RFC9493 Subject Identifiers to realm users
- Keycloak supports RFC 8935 Push-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Using HTTP
- Keycloak provides a SsfEventListener SPI that allows to react on SSF Events extracted from SETs.

 Non-Goals

Currently out of scope are the following features:
- Support for RFC8936 Poll-Based Security Event Token (SET) Delivery Using HTTP
- Support for Persistence of Security Events
- UI for managing stream configurations

The features mentioned above might be added at a later state.

 Discussion

 

 Notes

_No response_

Description

Use case / problem
We use Keycloak as a SAML broker/IdP in higher-ed. InCommon (Internet2) distributes signed federation metadata via the MDQ (per-entity) service and uses REFEDS entity categories (e.g., R&S) in md:EntityAttributes to automate attribute release and trust across institutions. Keycloak currently requires manual per-IdP imports and does not support automatic metadata refresh/MDQ, nor does it provide first-class support to emit/consume REFEDS entity categories. This makes it difficult to operate Keycloak in an InCommon/eduGAIN environment at scale.

 Value Proposition

This will allow Keycloak to operate natively with identity federations like InCommon and eduGain which are extensively used in higher education.

 Goals

Keycloak would be able to natively support SAML federations like InCommon. As part of this Keycloak could also support dynamically refreshing any SAML SP metadata which is required for this feature, but has its own benefits beyond this.

 Non-Goals

N/A

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

Were it up to me, I would have SAML federations be a button that can be selected under the Identity Providers' tab or have those configs be a separate section under the "SAML 2.0" form.

I have also attempted to locate a plugin that may provide this functionality, but havent found anything. As of right now, best I can tell, the easiest way to get federations working with Keycloak is to front keycloak with a small SP that will function as a proxy.

Description

Add native support for Cloudflare Turnstile as a CAPTCHA provider in Keycloak’s authentication flows. This would work similarly to the existing reCAPTCHA integration: administrators configure Turnstile keys in the Admin Console, Keycloak renders the widget on the login page, and the server validates the response with Cloudflare’s API during authentication.

 Value Proposition

- Provides a privacy-friendly alternative to reCAPTCHA, which many organizations prefer due to regional compliance or data processing concerns.
- Aligns naturally with deployments already using Cloudflare for WAF/CDN/DDoS protection.
- Reduces reliance on custom extensions for a very common requirement: CAPTCHA on login/registration flows.
- Improves user experience by leveraging Turnstile’s frictionless validation and lightweight widget.

 Goals

- A built-in CAPTCHA provider implementing the same SPI as reCAPTCHA.
- Admin Console configuration for:
 - Turnstile site key
 - Turnstile secret key
 - Widget mode (auto, managed, invisible)
 - Optional theme/style
- Rendering the Turnstile widget inside login forms via the theme system.
- Backend verification of the Turnstile token against the Cloudflare API.
- Compatibility with existing flows (e.g., browser, registration, reset-credentials) without additional customization.

 Non-Goals

- It should not replace or modify existing reCAPTCHA behavior.
- It should not add custom Cloudflare-specific rate-limiting or security logic beyond token verification.
- It should not handle Cloudflare account provisioning or automatic key management.
- It should not alter authentication flows beyond inserting the CAPTCHA step—flow design remains under admin control.
- It should not implement support for other CAPTCHA providers outside Turnstile (that would require separate proposals).

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

A plugin existed for this functionality but it's not maintained, someone has forked and has started adding new features but it would be nice to have the functionality built-in.

Description

As of 44255 the server maintains CredentialOfferState from the time of /credential-offer-uri until it expires. For a pre-auth CredentialOffer we provide the Wallet with a credential_identifier (through AuthorizationDetail attached to the AccessTokenResponse) that the Wallet can then reference in the CredentialRequest. At CredentialRequest time, we can then enforce all sorts of constraints that the Issuer set at the time of CredentialOffer creation.

Despite that and in general, the Wallet can always send a CredentialRequest that references a credential_configuration_id (instead of a credential_identifier) and hence bypass the CredentialOffer.

Similar to the pre-auth token, the server could attach Issuer state to the CredentialOffer and (if required by the credential configuration) the server could then reject a CredentialRequest that comes without reference to the associated CredentialOffer.

 Value Proposition

I suggest we put something in place that marks a given credential configuration as "requires credential offer"

 Goals

don't break existing functionality

In other words, once the application initiates the logout and provides id_token_hint, client_id as well as post_logout_redirect_uri, Keycloak silently logs a user out and finishes the entire flow with sending a redirect to Post Logout Page.

 STIG Compliance

 Per-Client logout setting that can be enforced across the Realm using Client Policies

 Non-Goals

 Per-Realm configuration options
