Description

It support OAuth CLient ID Metadata Document (CIMD) by persisting it to DB.
The document describes it in detail.

 Value Proposition

It is needed to support CIMD by keycloak.

 Goals

It covers persistent CIMD described in the document.

 Non-Goals

It does not cover other features like non-persistent CIMD other than persistent CIMD.

 Discussion

_No response_

 Reference
The referred specifications are as follows:

1. OAuth Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD) (version 00)
2. MCP: Authorization (2025-11-25 version)

 Requirements

The issue covers the following requirements of CIMD and MCP:
- Requirements whose requirement level is MUST or SHOULD.
- Requirements in Security Consideration.

 Specification

 Feature level
Experimental

 Client type
Both confidential and public client.

 Target requests including client_id
Authorization Request (the CIMD specification explicitly mentioned it).

 Client ID Verification
It chekcs if client_id parameter of an authorization request satisfies the requirements of the specifications.
For developlemt environment the following checks can be enable/disabled:
- Allow loopback address: allows IPv4/IPv6 loopback address
- Allow private address: allows private address
- Allow http scheme: allows http scheme of a URI 

 Client ID Validation
It chekcs if client_id parameter is valid according to the policy.

The CIMD and MCP specifications allow an authorization server to implement policies that determine the valid client_id parameter value. The CIMD and MCP specification show some examples of the policies roughly, but what policies are implemented in detail is up to the authorization server implementation. Therefore, the issue covers some of the following examples:
- Allow permitted domains: only allow a URI whose hostname is under the one of the permitted domain (wildcard can be used)

 Client Metadata Verification
It checks if client metadata satisfies the requirements of the specifications.

 Client Metadata Validation
It chekcs if client metadata is valid according to the policy.

The CIMD and MCP specifications allow an authorization server to implement policies that determine the valid client metadata. The CIMD and MCP specification show some examples of the policies roughly, but what policies are implemented in detail is up to the authorization server implementation. Therefore, the issue covers some of the following examples:
- Restrict same domain: only allow client_id and redirect_uri parameter of an authorization request whose hostname is under the one of the permitted domain (wildcard can be used).
- Required properties: only allow a client metadata that includes all required properties.
- Only Allow Confidential Client: only accept a confidential client.
- All URIs Restrict same domain: a client metadata includes properties whose values are URIs and an authorization server might access them. To prevent Server-side request forgery (SSRF), only allows these properties whose values are under the same domain of the permitted domains.

 Client Metadata Caching

 Create/update client metadata
The issue persists client metadata and update it. It treats the same as RFC 7591 OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration except for the following points:
- client_secret is not issued.
- A registration access token is not issued (to say more precisely, RFC 7592 OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration Management Protocol).

 Cache-Control header handling
The issue handles Cache-Control header in a client metadata response as follows:
- only consider directives of a response.
- do not consider whether private or public.
- consider max-age and s-maxage directives showing the lifetime of client metadata.
- s-maxage takes precedence over max-age (by following HTTP Cache-Control header specification).
- consider no-cache and no-store directives showing no caching client metadata.
- do not consider other directives.

 Process when a cache expires
Do nothing. After keycloak supports workflow for clients, it would be used to delete a client metadata.

 Displaying client info on grant screen
To mitigate the risk of phishing, the CIMD and MCP specifications requres an authorization server to show information on a client. The issue shows the following information on the client on the grant screen:
- client_id URL's hostname
- client_name
- A client logo via logo_uri
- A policy text via policy_uri
- Terms of service via tos_uri

 Tasks in the future
- Automatically Deleting persisted CIMD by Workflow
- Extending types of requests applied to CIMD
- Non-persistent CIMD
- Catching up with the newly released CIMD version
- Catching up with the newly released MCP version
- Promoting it to preview feature
- Promoting it to officially-supported feature

It chekcs if client metadata is valid according to the policy.

The CIMD and MCP specifications allow an authorization server to implement policies that determine the valid client metadata. The CIMD and MCP specification show some examples of the policies roughly, but what policies are implemented in detail is up to the authorization server implementation. Therefore, the issue covers some of the following examples:

SCIM provides standard APIs for managing users in an identity store, with an increasing amount of utilities, applications, and libraries supporting SCIM.

Keycloak should provide support to manage users through SCIM APIs

 Value Proposition

By providing SCIM REST APIs to manage users, groups, and roles in Keycloak it becomes easier to integrate Keycloak with a range of applications and libraries used for user management.

 Goals

 Support managing users through SCIM APIs
 Support managing groups and group mappings through SCIM APIs

Description

The OpenID Foundation started the AuthZEN [1] working group to provide standard mechanisms, protocols and formats to communicate authorization related information between components within one organization or across organizations, which may have been developed or sourced from different entities.

The working group is working on a specification to define an Authorization API [2]. This API enables Policy Decision Points (PDPs) and Policy Enforcement Points (PEPs) to communicate authorization requests and decisions to each other without requiring knowledge of each other's inner workings. The Authorization API is served by the PDP and is called by the PEP. The Authorization API includes an Evaluation endpoint, which provides specific access decisions. Other endpoints may be added in the future for other scenarios, including searching for subjects or resources.

Keycloak Authorization Services is a feature that enables a PDP [3] for individual resource servers (confidential clients) to evaluate authorization policies that govern access to their protected resources. This feature is already supported, and the underlying protocol is based on the User-Managed Access (UMA) specification. While at that time, UMA was the best/single standard describing an authorization protocol within the OAuth2 ecosystem, the work being done by the AuthZEN working group should provide a much better and simpler protocol.

After an initial study, the Authorization API specification seems to be very aligned with Keycloak's PDP, and we should be able to expose it based on it and eventually remove the dependency and support of UMA. By relying on a standard from the OpenID Foundation, we should increase the interoperability, adoption, and long-term support of our authorization capabilities.

 Value Proposition

The AuthZEN Authorization API is backed by the OpenID Foundation and should provide a simpler and more interoperable protocol to expose Keycloak's PDP. It has also been adopted by different vendors in the IAM space, and should put Keycloak in pace with these vendors while improving its authorization capabilities and helping our customers to better address their authorization requirements.

Given that the Keycloak's PDP provides most of the capabilities and semantics defined in the specification, we should be able to easily adopt yet another specification from the OpenID Foundation.

 Goals

- Expose the Keycloak Authorization Services PDP using the Authorization API
- Ability to evaluate authorization policies using the Authorization API
- Leverage the authorization model provided by Keycloak Authorization Services to manage resources, actions, and policies
- Examples and quickstart on how to evaluate authorization policies using the Authorization API
- Update the Keycloak Authorization Services to advertise support for the Authorization API
- The Authorization API should be an experimental feature
- Evaluate if we can consider deprecating/removing UMA support in future releases

 Non-Goals

- Any form of implementation of PEP is out of scope
- Have the Authorization API fully supported. That should only be possible once the standard is no longer a draft.
- Drop UMA support

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

_No response_

Description

Groups in Keycloak have a single parent. This constraint is blocking us to address common use cases where a group can be a child of different groups.

So far, two main components are impacted by this constraint:
 LDAP
 SCIM

In LDAP, group entries can reference, or be referenced by, different group entries so that a group can be a child of different groups. See [ 

In SCIM, the specification also makes it possible for a group to be a child of different parents. Similar to LDAP, the group schema defines child groups as a member therefore making it possible to share a group as a child of different groups. See [ For SCIM, this can be a potential blocker or impose limitations to fully support the specification.

In regards to use cases, supporting multiple parents for a group should avoid duplicating groups (and their permissions and members) when they might belong to different (sub) hierarchies. Therefore, improving the manageability of users and groups.

 Value Proposition

By supporting a group with multiple parents we should be able to:
 Extend our offerings to support more LDAP use cases and potentially increase our user/customer base
 More flexibility when enabling additional capabilities with a more flexible schema for groups, like SCIM.

 Goals

 A group can be a child of different groups
 The Admin Console updated to allow a group to be a member of multiple parents
 The Admin API updated to return and manage group representations where a group can be a member of multiple parents
 The import and export actions updated to represent/process groups with multiple parents
 The LDAP provider updated to import and manage groups with multiple parents
 Documentation updated as it states today that groups can only have a single parent

 Notes

 We might want to change the current group schema to remove the reference to the parent group. Instead, we should have a N:N mapping for a group and their members so that a group can be a child of multiple parents. See [ 
 The implementation should be based on the group schema defined by the SCIM specification in order to be based on an well-known and flexible standard
 We might want to enforce conditions to avoid cyclic relationships when a group is mapped as a child/parent of itself, or when a child group is mapped as a parent of its parent
kept_issues.body:
### Description

Groups in Keycloak have a single parent. This constraint is blocking us to address common use cases where a group can be a child of different groups.

So far, two main components are impacted by this constraint:
 * LDAP
 * SCIM

In LDAP, group entries can reference, or be referenced by, different group entries so that a group can be a child of different groups. See [https://github.com/keycloak/keycloak/issues/11752.]

In SCIM, the specification also makes it possible for a group to be a child of different parents. Similar to LDAP, the group schema defines child groups as a `member` therefore making it possible to share a group as a child of different groups. See [https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7643#page-25.] For SCIM, this can be a potential blocker or impose limitations to fully support the specification.

In regards to use cases, supporting multiple parents for a group should avoid duplicating groups (and their permissions and members) when they might belong to different (sub) hierarchies. Therefore, improving the manageability of users and groups.

### Value Proposition

By supporting a group with multiple parents we should be able to:
 * Extend our offerings to support more LDAP use cases and potentially increase our user/customer base
 * More flexibility when enabling additional capabilities with a more flexible schema for groups, like SCIM.

### Goals

 * A group can be a child of different groups
 * The Admin Console updated to allow a group to be a member of multiple parents
 * The Admin API updated to return and manage group representations where a group can be a member of multiple parents
 * The import and export actions updated to represent/process groups with multiple parents
 * The LDAP provider updated to import and manage groups with multiple parents
 * Documentation updated as it states today that groups can only have a single parent

### Notes

 * We might want to change the current group schema to remove the reference to the parent group. Instead, we should have a N:N mapping for a group and their members so that a group can be a child of multiple parents. See [https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7643#page-25|https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7643#page-25.].
 * The implementation should be based on the group schema defined by the SCIM specification in order to be based on an well-known and flexible standard
 * We might want to enforce conditions to avoid cyclic relationships when a group is mapped as a child/parent of itself, or when a child group is mapped as a parent of its parent

Description

Some customers operate Keycloak purely as an identity broker and therefore want to forbid local (realm) credentials entirely.
Today, the Browser flow always exposes the Username/Password form (unless apps push kc_idp_hint, or a custom theme/flow hides it), which confuses users and weakens some customers policy where users may try to log in locally while their policy mandates an authentication through IdP 2FA only. The existing behavior may also break the desired journeys for the Organizations feature where users should only select an organization IdP (or be auto-redirected to it if already linked).

 Value Proposition
Enable and Enforce IdP-only as as first-class login experience for users.
Security hardening: Removes local password surface; guarantees 2FA/MFA-backed SSO policies at upstream IdPs.
Cleaner, compliant broker-only journey for workforce and B2B/B2C organizations.

 Goals

- login screen shows IdP choices only (e.g., Azure AD for workforce, 'ItsMe' for externals), with no local username/password prompt anywhere in the flow.

- No local credentials across UIs:
-> Account Console: remove/disable Password, WebAuthn (as local), OTP as local configuration when IdP-only is enforced (unless explicitly allowed by admin, say via exception policy).
-> Admin Console: guardrails to prevent creating or resetting local passwords for users when the policy forbids it (with override only for admin break-glass, if configured).

- Backward compatibility:
-> Default behavior unchanged until IdP-only is enabled.
-> Works with existing themes (sane fallback) and honors IdP display hints/order.

 Non-Goals

- No forced client participation: feature must not require apps to pass kc_idp_hint or additional query params.
- No change to non-browser grants (client credentials, service accounts) or Admin REST auth. This proposal targets end-user browser SSO only.

Description

The clusterless feature was introduced in Keycloak 26.0 and has been verified to work alongside the supported multi-site deployment model. 

To cluster or not to cluster? This feature removes internal clustering from Keycloak, making each instance standalone and stateless. The caching layer is offloaded to an external Infinispan cluster.

 Advantages

 Lower memory consumption: Ideal for resource-constrained environments.
 Improved CPU efficiency: Instances no longer need to process JGroups traffic or handle requests from other nodes in a cluster.
 Faster startup times: Eliminates the need to rebalance, reconfigure, or transfer clustered cache data during boot.
 HPA friendly: Highly compatible with Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaling, allowing multiple pods to be started or stopped concurrently.
 Reliable upgrades: Simplifies zero-downtime upgrades by removing the internal clustering layer, which is a common source of failure during version transitions.

 Drawbacks
 Operational overhead: Requires an external Infinispan cluster to be deployed, configured, and managed.
 External dependency: While Keycloak provides tested default configurations for caches (see 32129), it adds a new component to the infrastructure stack.

 Other Important Information

 Shared Logic: The clusterless and multi-site features share the same underlying providers. Consequently, all test suites designed for multi-site are also executed against clusterless to ensure parity and stability.
 Session Management: This feature supports the persistent-user-sessions feature.
 Enabled: Sessions are stored in the database.
 Disabled: Sessions are stored in external caches.
 Single-Site Only: We are actively promoting the use of this feature for single-site deployments; however, comprehensive documentation for this specific use case is currently pending.

### Description

The `clusterless` feature was introduced in Keycloak 26.0 and has been verified to work alongside the supported `multi-site` deployment model. 

**To cluster or not to cluster?** This feature removes internal clustering from Keycloak, making each instance standalone and stateless. The caching layer is offloaded to an external Infinispan cluster.

#### Advantages

* **Lower memory consumption:** Ideal for resource-constrained environments.
* **Improved CPU efficiency:** Instances no longer need to process JGroups traffic or handle requests from other nodes in a cluster.
* **Faster startup times:** Eliminates the need to rebalance, reconfigure, or transfer clustered cache data during boot.
* **HPA friendly:** Highly compatible with Kubernetes Horizontal Pod Autoscaling, allowing multiple pods to be started or stopped concurrently.
* **Reliable upgrades:** Simplifies zero-downtime upgrades by removing the internal clustering layer, which is a common source of failure during version transitions.

#### Drawbacks
* **Operational overhead:** Requires an external Infinispan cluster to be deployed, configured, and managed.
* **External dependency:** While Keycloak provides tested default configurations for caches (see #32129), it adds a new component to the infrastructure stack.

### Other Important Information

* **Shared Logic:** The `clusterless` and `multi-site` features share the same underlying providers. Consequently, all test suites designed for `multi-site` are also executed against `clusterless` to ensure parity and stability.
* **Session Management:** This feature supports the `persistent-user-sessions` feature.
    * **Enabled:** Sessions are stored in the database.
    * **Disabled:** Sessions are stored in external caches.

Description

Currently, Keycloak’s brute force detection only triggers when there are repeated failed login attempts for the same user account. This allows the following attack scenario:
If an attacker possesses a list of email/password combinations, they can attempt authentication across many different user accounts without triggering the brute force protection, as long as each individual account is only tried a limited number of times.

The same applies to login attempts for non-existing user accounts. Repeated attempts do not trigger any lockout or detection mechanism.

Ideally repeated logins on multiple user accounts would trigger an (configurable) IP based lockout period preventing login attempts for all user accounts and a matching event informing administrators of this.

A workaround right now is rate limiting the relevant routes on the network / reverse proxy level, but a native Keycloak solution could give administrators additional information.

 Value Proposition

- Improve security for user accounts
- Prevent combo list attacks

 Goals

- Add additional configuration options for IP based brute force detection
- Update brute force protector to handle repeated login attempts on different user accounts from one IP 
- Add event to inform adminstrators 

 Non-Goals

- Prevent distributed attacks from multiple IPs

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

_No response_

### Description

Currently the value of http.httpsPort is used for the service definition and for the port that is used in the pods.

If for example 8443 is used as the port number, then the service definition looks like this:

```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: keycloak-service
...
spec:
...
  ports:
  - name: https
    port: 8443
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8443
...
```


and connections to the keycloak pods via the service now also must contain the 8443 port (e.g. https://keycloak-service.keycloak.svc:8443).

If there was a separate port number could be configured for the service, then it would be possible to use 443 for the service and thus simplify the URL to be https://keycloak-service.keycloak.svc

It would also be great if the name of the service was configurable (e.g. to avoid the -service suffix)

with configurable name and port the service definition could look like this:


```
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: keycloak
...
spec:
...
  ports:
  - name: https
    port: 443
    protocol: TCP
    targetPort: 8443
...
```

so that the URL becomes: https://keycloak.keycloak.svc



### Value Proposition

more flexibility for setting up keycloak via the keycloak operator. 
Would also be useful in migration scenarios (e.g. migrating from bitnami keycloak helm chart to keycloak operator)  where the service name should remain stable.

Description

There is currently no supported mechanism in Keycloak for seamlessly transferring an authenticated session from a native mobile application into an embedded WebView (or external browser) without re-prompting the user for credentials. Auth0 recently introduced a dedicated Native to Web SSO feature for this exact use case. This issue requests either native support for a similar flow or clear official documentation on how to achieve this with Keycloak.

 Value Proposition

This is a real and common problem for teams building mobile apps that embed web content requiring authentication. After researching how other apps handle this, every implementation I found is a custom, ad-hoc solution. There seems to be no established standard or recommended pattern. Therefore I treat this as a signal that the ecosystem is missing a well-defined, IdP-supported mechanism for this flow.
Auth0 solves this by issuing a short-lived Session Transfer Token (derived from a refresh token), which is then passed to the WebView and redeemed via the authorization endpoint to establish a cookie-based web session, without exposing long-lived tokens to the browser context.

 Goals

- Allow a native application with an active authenticated session to seamlessly transition a user into an embedded WebView or external browser without re-prompting for credentials
- Ensure the mechanism is secure by design: tokens used for session transfer must be short-lived, single-use, and ideally bound to a device or network identifier
- Avoid exposing long-lived credentials (e.g. refresh tokens) to the WebView or browser context at any point

 Non-Goals

- This is not intended to synchronize or share token state between the native app and the web app on an ongoing basis, it is a one-time session handoff
- This does not aim to replace or replicate the full OIDC authorization code flow with PKCE for native apps
- This is not intended to enable persistent or offline sessions in the WebView, a transient session is sufficient

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

 Reference Implementations:
- Auth0 Native to Web SSO
- Connect2Id Web session bootstrap for native apps

 Idea Dump
Option 1: Token Exchange with Offline Session Support
The native app passes its access token to the WebView, where the web app's backend accepts it, performs a Token Exchange to obtain a refresh token, and then establishes a cookie-based session.
Problem: Token Exchange currently does not support offline sessions. See: 44314. Until that is resolved, this approach is limited in practicality.

Option 2: Non-Standard Authorization Grant (Session Exchange)
Add a custom, non-standard authorization grant type, analogous to Auth0 Session Transfer Token flow, where the native client exchanges a refresh token for a short-lived, single-use session initiation token. The WebView then uses this token as part of a standard authorization code flow to obtain a web session.
This mirrors what Auth0 has done and keeps the UX seamless, but introduces a non-standard grant that would require careful security design (binding to IP/ASN, strict expiry, single-use enforcement).

Option 3: One-Time Action Tokens (Preferred)
Expose an additional endpoint where a native client (holding a valid session) can request a One-Time Token (Keycloak World: Action Token). This token is passed into the WebView, redeemed at a dedicated endpoint (Action Token Handler), and after verification, a transient browser session is created and the user is redirected to the web application fully authenticated, no credentials re-entered.
This feels like the most natural fit for Keycloak's existing architecture given Action Tokens are already a first-class concept. The scope is limited, the token is short-lived and single-use, and no long-lived credentials are ever exposed to the WebView's browser context.

Description

Add a supported configuration option to disable local username/password login on the Keycloak login screen and display only Identity Provider login options without auto redirecting to the IdP. While Keycloak supports IdP integration , there is currently no way to enforce an IdP-only login experience while still presenting the Keycloak login UI.

Based on the current authentication flow behavior:

- The Username Password Form Authenticator is responsible for rendering the login screen itself, removing or disabling this step results in no login UI at all and consequently IdP login buttons are also not shown.
- Using Identity Provider redirector as REQUIRED causes Keycloak to immediately redirect to the IdP, completely bypassing the login page.

As a result there is no built in way to:

- Keep the Keycloak login screen 
- Remove or disable local username/password login
- Still present IdP login options to the user

Custom themes can hide the username/password fields visually but this is a UI-only workaround and does not provide enforced behavior.

 Value Proposition

- Enforce IdP only authentication
- Improve security by preventing local credential based login
- Retain the keycloak login page for supporting multi-IdP selection

 Goals

- Render the standard Keycloak login page
- Disable or hide local username/password input fields
- Display only configured Identity Provider login buttons

 Non-Goals

- No change in existing auto redirect behaviour
- No custom themes or authentication flow customization
- Do not remove local authentication entirely from Keycloak

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

_No response_

Description

In Kubernetes clusters utilizing policy engines or mutating admission webhooks (such as Kyverno or OPA/Gatekeeper), labels are frequently injected automatically into Pods for organizational tagging, network policies, or observability.

For StatefulSet-managed workloads (like Keycloak), this creates a critical conflict:
1. The Keycloak Operator creates a StatefulSet.
2. Kubernetes locks the spec.selector.matchLabels as immutable upon creation.
3. An admission controller (Kyverno) injects a label (e.g., team: platform) into the Pod template metadata at admission time.
4. The resulting Pod template labels no longer match the immutable selector.

This leads to a permanent reconciliation error in the operator:
> StatefulSet.apps "keycloak" is invalid: spec.selector: Invalid value: ... field is immutable

Currently, users have to resort to the unsupported pod template override, which is fragile, bypasses validation, and isn't semantically designed for this purpose.

 Value Proposition

Introduce a podLabels field within the SchedulingSpec of the Keycloak Custom Resource (CR).

By allowing users to declare these labels directly in the CR, the Operator can include them in the StatefulSet selector from the very first reconciliation. When the admission controller later "injects" the same labels, there is no divergence—the Pod template and the selector remain perfectly consistent.

 Example Configuration
kept_issues.body:
### Description

In Kubernetes clusters utilizing policy engines or mutating admission webhooks (such as **Kyverno** or **OPA/Gatekeeper**), labels are frequently injected automatically into Pods for organizational tagging, network policies, or observability.

For **StatefulSet-managed workloads** (like Keycloak), this creates a critical conflict:
1. The Keycloak Operator creates a `StatefulSet`.
2. Kubernetes locks the `spec.selector.matchLabels` as **immutable** upon creation.
3. An admission controller (Kyverno) injects a label (e.g., `team: platform`) into the Pod template metadata at admission time.
4. The resulting Pod template labels no longer match the immutable selector.

This leads to a permanent reconciliation error in the operator:
> `StatefulSet.apps "keycloak" is invalid: spec.selector: Invalid value: ... field is immutable`

Currently, users have to resort to the `unsupported` pod template override, which is fragile, bypasses validation, and isn't semantically designed for this purpose.



### Value Proposition

Introduce a `podLabels` field within the `SchedulingSpec` of the Keycloak Custom Resource (CR).

By allowing users to declare these labels directly in the CR, the Operator can include them in the `StatefulSet` selector from the very first reconciliation. When the admission controller later "injects" the same labels, there is no divergence—the Pod template and the selector remain perfectly consistent.

### Example Configuration
```yaml
apiVersion: k8s.keycloak.org/v2alpha1
kind: Keycloak
metadata:
  name: keycloak
spec:
  scheduling:
    podLabels:
      team: platform
      monitoring: enabled
```
kept_issues.title: [Feature] Support custom Pod labels in SchedulingSpec to prevent reconciliation conflicts

Description

This issue proposes to add Shared Signals Framework support to Keycloak in the SSF Transmitter role. 
Keycloak signs Security Event Tokens (SETs, RFC 8417) describing realm/user/session/credential events and
delivers them to OAuth clients registered as SSF Receivers, either by HTTP PUSH (RFC 8935) or HTTP POLL (RFC 8936).

The implementation targets the OpenID Shared Signals Framework 1.0 (Final) specification plus the CAEP Interoperability Profile 1.0.
To support compatibility with Apple Business Manager / Apple School Manager, we must also support
the legacy Shared Signals and Events Framework.

This feature should be put behind a Profile.Feature.SSF flag and market experimental.

Originally proposed (Receiver-side) in 43614; pivoted to ship the Transmitter first because it covers 
the strongest community asks and gives us a working SSF foundation to validate against real receivers
before we tackle the Receiver-side action-mapping design.

 Value Proposition

- Lets Keycloak broadcast user-lifecycle events to downstream SaaS in near real time instead of relying on per-app polling, short-lived token TTLs, or vendor-specific webhooks. A logout in Keycloak can sign a user out of every connected SaaS within seconds; a credential change can invalidate cached sessions elsewhere; an admin-initiated session revoke can drop device fleets immediately.
- Unlocks the Apple Business Manager / Apple School Manager integration story. ABM/ASM is a concrete, customer-facing drive-use case where Keycloak-as-IdP needs to push CAEP session-revoked SETs so Apple devices honour the revocation. We ship the legacy SSE CAEP profile narrowing alongside SSF 1.0 so a single transmitter serves both modern SSF receivers and Apple's pre-SSF-1.0 wire shape.
- Positions Keycloak inside the emerging cross-vendor identity signal ecosystem. SSF / CAEP / RISC are increasingly an
 interoperability baseline (caep.dev conformance suite, vendor matrices). Shipping the transmitter now lets Keycloak appear in these matrices and gives the community a Keycloak-native event source they can pair with any SSF-capable receiver.
- Adds a first-class extension seam for non-Keycloak event sources. The synthetic-emit endpoint lets external systems
 (LDAP password notifiers, MDM compliance changes, fraud-detection signals) flow through the same signed SET pipeline, so a Keycloak deployment becomes the SSF delivery hub for an entire identity ecosystem rather than just for events Keycloak observes itself.

 Goals

- SSF 1.0 stream management CRUD, status transitions, verification, subjects (per SSF 8.1).
- SET delivery via HTTP PUSH (RFC 8935) and HTTP POLL (RFC 8936) POLL in a return-immediately form.
- Robust event delivery via lean persistent JPA outbox (SSF_PENDING_EVENT) with cluster-aware drainer, exponential backoff, and dead-lettering.
- CAEP credential-change (UPDATE_CREDENTIAL) / session-revoked (LOGOUT with filter) event mapping from native Keycloak events.
- Subject selection: per-user / per-org ssf.notify. attribute, default_subjects=ALL/NONE policy, SSF 9.3 malicious-subject-removal grace-window defense.
- Synthetic event emit endpoint so non-Keycloak event sources (LDAP, MDM, custom integrations) can route through the transmitter.
- Per-receiver "manual-only events" gate to suppress auto-emit per event type per receiver.
- Legacy SSE CAEP profile SSF event narrowing for Apple Business / School Manager interop.
- Per-realm SSF admin REST + admin-console SSF tab on SSF-enabled clients (Receiver / Stream / Subjects / Pending Events sub-tabs).
- Expose metrics under keycloak_ssf_.
- Three-level feature gating (server Profile.Feature.SSF, realm ssf.transmitterEnabled, client ssf.enabled).
- Integration test coverage.

 Non-Goals

- SSF Receiver role for Keycloak ingestion of inbound SETs from upstream IdPs / risk engines is intentionally out of scope for the experimental cut. 
- POLL long-polling (returnImmediately=false, maxWait) every poll returns immediately. Honouring long-poll on today's HTTP layer would pin platform threads from the worker pool; deferred until Keycloak's HTTP handlers can run on virtual threads.
- Multiple streams per receiver capped at one stream per receiver client. Most vendor SSF implementations cap the same way; a workaround for genuinely multi-stream needs is to model each stream as its own OAuth receiver client.
- Dedicated SSF signing key the transmitter shares the realm's OIDC token-signing key for now. A separate realm-key provider plus a separate JWKS slice will land in a follow-up so receivers can pin the SSF key independently of OIDC rotation cadence.
- CAEP §2.6 RSA ≥ 2048 enforcement at the SSF layer relies on the realm's signing-key configuration today; the transmitter does not refuse to sign with an undersized key. 
- Performance characterization, security review, formal interop matrix those are the GA prerequisites tracked under the
 supported-milestone follow-ups, not part of this experimental delivery.
- User-facing documentation the internal design doc is the reference for this milestone; promotion to user-facing docs lands with the tech-preview milestone.

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

Issue 43614 originally proposed the Receiver role; the pivot rationale is captured in the Description above.
This also solves 14217 by adding support for emitting RISC and CAEP events.

Description

The EUDI-Wallet will be introduced EU-wide starting 2027, enabling EU-citizens to prove their identity to (government) online services and store/present attestations in a secure wallet on their phone. Public Authorities must support the wallet based on eIDAS 2.0 regulation.

Keycloak is currently implementing the issuance side of this: Define, store and issue credentials to OID4VCI-compatible wallets.
The other side is currently not handled by Keycloak at all though: using identity credentials (like ID cards, called "PID" in this ecosystem) to authenticate users. Authentication is one of if not the primary use case for using Keycloak, so being able to use wallet credentials for authentication is IMHO even more important than issuing credentials when using Keycloak.

I implemented a verifier extension for Keycloak and tested it successfully in the german test environment (called "Sandbox" by SPRIND): 
When talking to other potential users of this in the public sector, i quickly realized though, that the general expectation is for Keycloak to provide this out-of-the-box. Extensions are not usable in all environments, keeping them up-to-date with the rapid development of the OID4VC-foundations inside Keycloak is hard and supporting multiple Keycloak versions in parallel is not something we can handle at all.

As part of the OAuth-SIG working group for OID4VCI, i proposed to take this extension as inspiration and re-implement the verifier functionality in Keycloak itself with help of other SIG-members like @tdiesler 

The main question that remains now is the timeline. Since downstream services that depend on this functionality have to be operational in 01/2027, i strongly believe that this work must not be delayed any further.

 Value Proposition

Support OID4VP to allow users to authenticate with wallet credentials like a PID or some custom credential (EAA).

 Goals

- Provide OID4VP/Wallet identity provider implementation as part of Keycloak (See notes for the reasoning behind that choice)
- Pass all OID4VP conformance tests including HAIP 1.0
- Support detecting revoked credentials using the Token Status List specification
- Support different trust anchors, i.e. realm certificates for credentials issued by Keycloak itself, ETSI trust lists for credentials issued by other EUDI-issuers and (optionally, when HAIP is not enforced, see notes below) JWKS-lookup using the .well-known/jwt-vc-issuer endpoint
- Support optional parts of OID4VP that are required for the EUDI-ecosystem, especially sending registration certificates via verifier_info in the Authentication Request
- Support credential_sets (optional part of DCQL) to request multiple credentials at once, while one or more of them could be optional. (This will be needed a lot for example in Germany, where the PID-credentials do not have any identifying claim. So authentication with high LoA will be achieved by requesting the PID + a custom login credential)

 Non-Goals

- Support optional parts of the relevant specifications that are not used in the EUDI-wallet ecosystem, like transaction_data or unused client identifier prefixes/schemes: openid_federation, decentralized_identifier, verifier_attestation, origin
- Support other use cases for verification than logging in out-of-the box (credentials that attest some kind of business state, like employment status, and are not suited for user authentication)
- Integrate wallet login into the login flow itself, like WebAuthn, using the Digital Credentials API (browser adoption is still very limited but this could/should be a follow up later on)

 Discussion

 

 Notes

I propose to implement this as an identity provider, because i think that this makes the implementation a lot easier than doing this as an authenticator (there is a lot of back-and-forth communication between the RP and the wallet after all and identity providers already support this with their own endpoints). Also identity provider mappers are a good way to get data out of the credential and map it to the user or session (and that is something that will be needed in a lot of cases).
In our extension, we also generate the DCQL-query to the wallet directly from mapper configuration which allows for a much better user experience for administrators than hand-writing it.
But you could also argue that authenticators are a better fit because we are not really delegating authentication but request a credential that we validate ourself. Using authenticators would also make later usage of the Digital Credentials API easier, because that works a lot like WebAuthn/Passkeys.

Furthermore, the EUDI-ecosystem requires HAIP-compliance but it might be useful to also support Non-HAIP scenarios. This is relevant when choosing trust anchors for example, because Non-HAIP allows JWKS-lookup via .well-known/jwt-vc-issuer while HAIP forbids this and enforces usage of the certificate-chain provided in the x5c-claim.

See also this issue for ETSI trust list support: 

 Visualization

The following is a simplified visualization of the flow between Keycloak and the Wallet. All of those steps have different variants like call-by-reference / value for the Authentication Request, optional encryption of the Request Object as well as the Wallet-Response (vp_token) and other intricacies of the specifications.

The goal of this image is to just give a general idea of how this thing is supposed to work

Description

Hi,

We are looking for a way to integrate an external registration form with Keycloak.

The idea would be:

- The user submits a registration form in our web app.
- The web app sends the data to Keycloak through the REST API.
- The user remains pending until an admin reviews and approves the request.
- After approval, the user receives an email to set/change the password on first login.

From what I have found, Keycloak supports creating users through the Admin REST API, disabling/enabling users, and sending required action emails such as UPDATE_PASSWORD, but I do not see a native “pending approval” state for registrations.

Is there any recommended workaround for this?

For example, would it make sense to create the user as disabled, store some custom attributes, and later enable the account manually after admin approval? Or is this expected to be handled outside Keycloak?

Thanks.

 Value Proposition

This would help teams that cannot allow open self-registration, but still need a controlled onboarding process initiated from an external application.

 Goals

The feature should allow external applications to submit user registration requests through the REST API and keep them pending until an admin approves or rejects them.

After approval, the user should be activated and receive an email to complete required actions such as setting/changing the password or verifying the email.

 Non-Goals

.

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

_No response_

Description

Allow UserStorageProvider implementations to opt into storing service account users.

Currently UserStorageManager.addUser hardcodes all service-account- users to local JPA storage, and getServiceAccount only consults local storage, regardless of what user federation providers are configured for the realm. This change introduces an optional capability interface, UserServiceAccountProvider, that a storage provider can implement to take ownership of service account creation and lookup. When such a provider is enabled, UserStorageManager routes service account users to it (in priority order) before falling back to local storage. Realms without a UserServiceAccountProvider are unaffected.

 Value Proposition

Deployments that use an external user store as the single source of truth (custom DB, IdM platform, etc.) currently end up with a split-brain: human users live in the external store while service account users are forced into Keycloak's local DB. This causes issues in several real-world setups:
- Stateless / read-only Keycloak deployments where the local DB is treated as disposable config and all identities must come from the external store. Today, enabling service accounts on a client silently writes a user row to the local DB.
- Centralized governance / audit where compliance requires all identities (both human and machine) to be inventoried, provisioned, and de-provisioned through one system.
- Multi-cluster / multi-region deployments that share a federated user store but run separate Keycloak databases; service account IDs and role mappings diverge between clusters.

This proposal is purely additive and opt-in meaning existing providers and realms see no behavioral change.

 Goals

- A capability interface (UserServiceAccountProvider) a UserStorageProvider can implement to handle addServiceAccountUser and getServiceAccount.
- UserStorageManager consults implementing providers in priority order, falling back to local storage when none handle the request.
- AbstractUserAdapter / AbstractUserAdapterFederatedStorage permit overriding get/setServiceAccountClientLink so adapters can persist the client link externally.
- Federated-storage cleanup (preRemove) runs for externally stored service accounts on client deletion.

 Non-Goals

- Changing the default behavior, we want service accounts to remain local unless a provider explicitly opts in.
- Making the built-in LDAP provider implement this interface.
- Promoting this to the public server-spi (it lives in server-spi-private until the contract is proven).
- Migrating existing locally stored service accounts to an external provider.

 Discussion

 

 Notes

The implementation for this proposal is small and self-contained: one new interface in server-spi-private, a routing change in UserStorageManager, and relaxed Javadoc on the two abstract adapters. Any code change would include an integration test (ServiceAccountUserStorageTest) with a reference in-memory provider exercising create → client_credentials grant → client delete.

Description

 Summary
Keycloak has no built-in authenticator that adjusts the authentication 
flow based on a user's recent login failure history. The brute force 
subsystem tracks failures via UserLoginFailureModel, but there is no 
mechanism to use that data to dynamically escalate authentication 
within a flow.

 Problem
When a user account has experienced repeated login failures, there is 
no way for administrators to require stronger authentication for that 
specific user without applying that requirement globally to all users.

 Proposed Solution
Add a new Authenticator SPI implementation, RiskScoreAuthenticator, 
that reads the user's recent login failure count and escalates to an 
OTP challenge when failures reach a configurable threshold (default: 3). 
If failures are below the threshold, the authenticator passes through 
without interruption.

 Files Added
- RiskScoreAuthenticator.java (authenticator logic)
- RiskScoreAuthenticatorFactory.java (SPI factory registration)
- Updated META-INF/services/org.keycloak.authentication.AuthenticatorFactory
- RiskScoreAuthenticatorTest.java (integration tests)

 Value Proposition

Keycloak applies the same authentication flow to every login attempt
regardless of how many times that user has recently failed. This means
a suspicious login after repeated failures receives no additional
friction, while all legitimate users face the same static experience.

The RiskScoreAuthenticator closes this gap by reading a user's recent
login failure count and requiring OTP only when the count reaches a
configured threshold. Users with no failure history log in without
interruption. Accounts that have triggered repeated failures are
challenged with a second factor automatically, without any changes
to the global authentication policy.

 Goals

- Read the user's recent login failure count from UserLoginFailureModel
 during the authentication flow
- Escalate to an OTP challenge when the failure count reaches or
 exceeds the configured threshold (default: 3)
- Pass through without interruption when the failure count is below
 the threshold
- Register as a pluggable Authenticator SPI step that administrators
 can add to any authentication flow via the Admin UI
- Integrate with the existing AuthenticationProcessor chain without
 modifying it

 Non-Goals

- Does not replace or modify Keycloak's existing brute force protection
- Does not evaluate other risk signals such as IP address, device
 fingerprint, or login time
- Does not block login attempts outright; escalation is limited to
 requiring OTP
- Does not add new Admin Console screens beyond the existing flow
 editor
- Does not support per-client or per-user threshold configuration
 in this version

 Discussion

_No response_

 Notes

_No response_

1. This feature can create SAML identity providers using stateless SSO(Just-In time) provisioning in Keycloak.
2. This feature can peform direct OAuth token exchange with SAML IDPs by accepting valid SAML assertion.
3. This fetaure can leverage Keycloak in-built client(protocol) mappers capability to create custom attributes from SAML response in OAuth token.
